summary: Updates the Cryptographic Message Syntax of RFC 5652 so that algorithm identifiers in signed-data and authenticated-data content are adequately protected. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: A signed letter should also cover the note saying how it was signed, or a trickster could change that note. This document makes sure the signing method note is protected too.

questions: how to protect algorithm identifiers in cms
what is an algorithm substitution attack
what does rfc 8933 change in rfc 5652
why must cms use the same digest algorithm
subtitle: Closes a gap in CMS signatures so attackers cannot swap the hash algorithm behind a signed message.

tldr.problem: CMS signed-data, unlike an X.509 certificate, does not protect its algorithm identifiers, so an attacker could try to substitute a weaker algorithm that gives the same result.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC requires the same digest algorithm for the content digest and the digest of the signed attributes, and recommends including the CMSAlgorithmProtection attribute in signed and authenticated attributes.
tldr.outcome: Algorithm substitution attacks become significantly more difficult. Protection is still missing for several other CMS content types, which the RFC leaves as future work.

facts.label: Mandated
facts.value: Same digest algorithm for content and signed attributes

today: RFC 8933 is a Proposed Standard from October 2020. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and it updates RFC 5652.

sections.title: Algorithm Substitution Attacks
sections.content:
This RFC updates the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) of RFC 5652 so that algorithm identifiers in the signed-data and authenticated-data content types are adequately protected. An X.509 certificate protects its algorithm identifier and parameters by signing them. CMS signed-data does not, so it can be vulnerable to an algorithm substitution attack, where the attacker changes the identifier or its parameters to alter how the recipient verifies.

The attacker looks for a different algorithm that produces the same result. For example, if the signer used SHA-256, the attacker looks for a weaker hash that also produces a 256-bit result and hopes to find a message with the same hash value, a cross-algorithm collision. A second case arises when a digest is larger than the signature algorithm needs and is reduced: with SHA-512 and ECDSA with the P-256 curve, the attacker only has to collide with the first half of the digest. Parameterized identifiers, such as randomized hash functions, give the attacker values to manipulate as well.
sections.eli5: If a teacher checks your homework with one answer key, a cheater might slip in an easier key. This RFC makes sure the key you used is locked in.

sections.title: The Two Updates
sections.content: The RFC makes two changes to CMS. First, it mandates a convention that many implementations already follow: the originator MUST use the same hash algorithm to compute the digest of the message content and the digest of the signed attributes. Second, it recommends that the originator include the CMSAlgorithmProtection attribute from RFC 6211.
sections.eli5: There is one firm rule, use the same hash tool for both steps, and one strong suggestion, write down which tools you used inside the signed part.

sections.title: Required Use of the Same Hash Algorithm
sections.content:
Three passages of RFC 5652 change. In Section 5.3, the description of digestAlgorithm now says that if signedAttrs is present, the same digest algorithm MUST be used for the digest of the eContent (carried in the message-digest attribute) and for the digest of the DER-encoded signedAttrs, which is passed to the signature algorithm. Section 5.4 gains a paragraph saying the same thing. In Section 5.6, the recipient's calculation of the content digest must use that same algorithm for the eContent and the message-digest attribute.

Because the signature covers the signed attributes, this forces an attacker to mount a hash substitution attack on the overall signature, not only on the content digest.
sections.eli5: If you use one kind of seal for the envelope and the label, a forger has to fake the seal for both, not just one.

sections.title: Compatibility Considerations
sections.content:
The new rule could break implementations that used different digest algorithms for the content and for the signed attributes. Signatures they produced would be considered invalid by an implementation following this RFC. The RFC says that most, if not all, implementations already require the same algorithm for both.

Timestamping needs special handling. When an originator does not want to share the content with a Time Stamping Authority (TSA), it sends a MessageImprint with its own digest. When producing the TimeStampToken, the TSA MUST use the same digest algorithm for the eContent and the message-digest attribute. To keep older tokens valid, the TSA is not required to match the algorithm of the MessageImprint embedded in the TSTInfo.
sections.eli5: A few old systems did it differently, but almost nobody does. Timestamp helpers get a small exception so older timestamps still count.

sections.title: The CMSAlgorithmProtection Attribute
sections.content: A paragraph is added to Section 14 of RFC 5652. It says there are no known algorithm substitution attacks today, but listing the originator's algorithm identifiers as a signed or authenticated attribute makes such an attack significantly more difficult. So an originator of signed-data that includes signed attributes SHOULD include the CMSAlgorithmProtection attribute among them. An originator of authenticated-data that includes authenticated attributes SHOULD do the same.
sections.eli5: Writing 'I used these tools' inside the locked part of the letter means anyone who changes the tools breaks the lock.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
For signed-data, the changes force an attacker to attack the hash algorithm of the overall signature. For authenticated-data, they force a MAC algorithm substitution attack, which is hard because the attacker does not know the authentication key.

Some signature algorithms stop hash substitution by feeding a digest algorithm identifier into the signature. Citing a 2002 paper, the RFC says this firewall may not work with newer algorithms: RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 protects the digest identifier, but RSASSA-PSS does not. A signer therefore still needs a way to tell recipients which digest algorithms are allowed, for example through an X.509v3 certificate extension.

The attribute gives no protection for the enveloped-data, digested-data, encrypted-data or authenticated-enveloped-data content types. A mechanism for those is left as work for the future. The RFC has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: The lock now covers two kinds of letters. Some other kinds of letters are still unlocked, and fixing them is a job for later.
